summary: This document describes how to avoid IP fragmentation of large IKEv2 messages. This lets IKEv2 messages pass through network devices that drop IP fragments.

eli5.summary: A big package that does not fit through a narrow door can be split into smaller boxes. This RFC lets secure-connection setup messages be cut into smaller pieces so they get through.

questions: why do ike messages get dropped by nat
what is the encrypted fragment payload
subtitle: How IKEv2 splits its own large messages into smaller encrypted pieces so they get past devices that drop IP fragments.

tldr.problem: Large IKEv2 messages, especially IKE_AUTH with certificates, can exceed the path MTU and be fragmented by IP, but some network devices such as NAT boxes drop IP fragments, so the IPsec Security Association is never established.
tldr.mechanism: IKEv2 splits the content of an Encrypted payload into chunks before encryption and sends each as its own IKE Fragment message, using a new Encrypted Fragment payload (type 53). Support is negotiated with a notification of type 16430.
tldr.outcome: Each fragment is individually protected and small enough to avoid IP fragmentation. Messages without an Encrypted payload, such as IKE_SA_INIT, cannot be fragmented this way.

today: RFC 7383 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the IKEv2 fragmentation mechanism that builds on RFC 7296.

sections.title: The Problem with IP Fragmentation
sections.content:
IKEv2 (RFC 7296) runs over UDP. Most of its messages are small, usually below several hundred bytes, but the IKE_AUTH exchange can need messages of up to several KB, especially when certificates are sent. When a message exceeds the path MTU it is fragmented at the IP level, and some network devices, notably some NAT boxes, do not let IP fragments through. That blocks IKE and stops the peers from establishing an IPsec Security Association.

The RFC adds that Carrier-Grade NATs are meant to support receiving fragments, but the memory cost is high and some ISPs use equipment that drops them anyway. Many operators also filter all IPv6 fragments. A study cited in the RFC sent packets fragmented to the minimum MTU of 1280 to 502 IPv6 probes and found that ten percent of the probes did not receive fragmented packets in any given trial period.
sections.eli5: Some gatekeepers on the road refuse any parcel that arrives in pieces. If your message is too big, it never arrives, and the two sides cannot start talking securely.

sections.title: The Idea and Its Limits
sections.content:
Instead of letting IP split a big message, IKEv2 splits it itself into smaller IKE Fragment messages, so the resulting IP datagrams are small enough to avoid IP fragmentation. Fragmentation happens before the original message is encrypted and authenticated, so every fragment is protected individually. The receiver collects, verifies and decrypts the fragments and merges them back into the original content.

This has limits. Because fragments are cryptographically protected, the keys SK_a and SK_e must already exist, so a message can be fragmented only if it contains an Encrypted payload. IKE_SA_INIT messages therefore cannot be fragmented, and neither can the IKE_SESSION_RESUME messages of RFC 5723. Also, the smallest IP datagram carrying an IKE Fragment is about 100 bytes, depending on the algorithms, while the guaranteed unfragmentable IPv4 size from RFC 791 is 68 bytes. Such tiny path MTUs are described as very rare.
sections.eli5: Instead of letting the post office chop your parcel, you cut it into small sealed boxes first. But you can only do that after the secret lock is set up, so the very first hello messages cannot be split this way.

sections.title: Negotiation and When to Use It
sections.content:
The initiator signals support by putting a Notify payload of type IKEV2_FRAGMENTATION_SUPPORTED in its IKE_SA_INIT request. If the responder supports and wants the extension, it includes the same notification in its response. In the notification, Protocol ID and SPI Size MUST be 0 and Notify Message Type MUST be 16430. It carries no data.

IKE fragmentation MUST NOT be used unless both peers have indicated support. After that, the initiator of each exchange decides. It might send unfragmented first and fall back to fragments after several retransmissions with no complete response, always fragment, or fragment only large messages. The guidelines are:

  • A peer that has reason to think IP fragmentation will interfere SHOULD use IKE fragmentation. The hint may come from a lower layer, configuration or heuristics.
  • If fragmentation was already used in this IKE SA, a peer SHOULD keep using it for messages above the fragmentation threshold.
  • It SHOULD NOT be used where IP fragmentation of both request and response is unlikely, for example liveness checks.
  • Otherwise the responder SHOULD answer in the same form as the request.

In most cases it will be used in the IKE_AUTH exchange, especially with certificates.
sections.eli5: Both sides first say 'I can handle small boxes.' Only if both say yes do they use them, and they skip it for tiny messages that would never need it.

sections.title: The Encrypted Fragment Payload
sections.content:
The Encrypted Fragment payload, written SKF, has payload type 53 and is also called the Encrypted and Authenticated Fragment payload. The original, unencrypted content of the Encrypted payload is treated as a binary blob and cut into chunks regardless of inner payload boundaries. Each chunk is then encrypted and authenticated exactly as in Section 3.14 of RFC 7296. Like the Encrypted payload, SKF MUST be the last payload in the message.

Besides the standard payload header, SKF adds two 16-bit fields:

  • Fragment Number: the number of this fragment, starting from 1. It MUST NOT be zero and MUST be less than or equal to Total Fragments.
  • Total Fragments: how many fragments the message was divided into. It MUST NOT be zero.

In the first fragment, Next Payload MUST be the type of the first inner payload. In all later fragments it MUST be zero. Each fragment's IKE header is copied intact from the original message except for Length (adjusted) and Next Payload (set to the first payload in that fragment, usually SKF). If a future extension mixes unprotected payloads with an Encrypted payload, all the unprotected payloads MUST go in the first fragment, and SKF MUST be present in every fragment even if it ends up carrying no data.
sections.eli5: Each small box has a label saying 'box 2 of 5', and only the first box says what kind of thing is inside. Every box is locked on its own.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Fragments
sections.content:
Choosing the size. The sender SHOULD pick chunk sizes so each IP datagram stays under a fragmentation threshold. If it knows the path MTU it SHOULD use it. Otherwise it is RECOMMENDED to use 1280 bytes as the maximum datagram size for IPv6 and 576 bytes for IPv4, possibly less if tunnels are on the path. The RFC calls 576 a compromise: large enough for this scheme and small enough to avoid fragmentation in most situations.

PMTU discovery is OPTIONAL, since IKE produces little traffic. If implemented, it follows Section 10.4 of RFC 4821 but searches downward: the initiator starts from larger thresholds and refragments with the next smaller one when no response arrives after several retransmissions. The Total Fragments value MUST increase with each new probe, which lets the receiver tell fragment sets apart and restart reassembly when a newer set arrives.

Receiving. The receiver silently discards a fragment if Fragment Number or Total Fragments is zero, if Fragment Number exceeds Total Fragments, if Total Fragments is lower than that of stored fragments, if it is a replay (same Message ID, Fragment Number and Total Fragments), or if the Integrity Check Value fails. When all fragments have arrived, their decrypted contents are merged and the result is processed like a normal IKE message. If fragments do not all arrive before a timeout, they are all discarded: the initiator retransmits or gives up as in RFC 7296, and the responder acts as if no request arrived.

Replay and retransmission detection use Fragment Number and Total Fragments together with the Message ID. A retransmitted request fragment only triggers a retransmitted response if its Fragment Number is 1.
sections.eli5: The sender cuts the message to a size that fits the narrowest road it knows about, trying smaller sizes if nothing gets through. The receiver checks each box is genuine and new, and only opens the whole thing once every box is there.

sections.title: Other Extensions and Transport Effects
sections.content:
IKE fragmentation is described as compatible with most IKE extensions, including IKE Session Resumption (RFC 5723) and Quick Crash Detection (RFC 6290). Because IKE_SESSION_RESUME messages have no Encrypted payload and can be large due to the ticket, the RFC suggests smaller tickets, for example a 'ticket by reference' instead of 'ticket by value'. For the High Availability protocol support of RFC 6311, IKE Message ID Synchronization messages MUST NOT be sent fragmented, to make replay detection easier.

Fragments are not individually acknowledged; the response fragments are sent together only once the whole request is reassembled and processed. If any single fragment is lost, the message cannot be reassembled, so delivery becomes somewhat less likely, which may matter on lossy networks. Implementations MAY use longer timeouts and more retransmits before considering the peer dead.
sections.eli5: If one small box goes missing, the whole parcel cannot be rebuilt, so on bumpy roads it is worth waiting a bit longer and trying again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Most considerations match base IKEv2. Since each fragment is individually authenticated, the receiver can check it on its own, which protects peers against a DoS attack. Avoiding IP fragmentation also removes the risk, noted in RFC 7296, of exhausting IP reassembly buffers.

A new attack is possible, though: an attacker completes IKE_SA_INIT, computes SK_a and SK_e, then sends a large but incomplete set of IKE_AUTH fragments. They pass the ICV check and fill reassembly buffers until they time out. To limit this, receivers are RECOMMENDED to cap the total decrypted size of queued fragments, and if a peer exceeds it, SHOULD drop the connection and discard the fragments. The RFC says the cap is NOT RECOMMENDED to exceed 64 KB. Receivers should also not act on partially reassembled payloads, because missing fragments could change their meaning.

IANA registers payload type 53 (Encrypted and Authenticated Fragment, SKF) and notify type 16430 (IKEV2_FRAGMENTATION_SUPPORTED).
sections.eli5: A cheater could send lots of boxes but never the last one, to fill your shelves. So you set a limit on how much you will store before you stop listening.
